quests.instruction: In an interview you hear “So, tell me about your last job.” Which spoken form of “about your” fits?
quests.word: So, tell me about your last job
quests.textToSpeak: So, tell me about your last job
options: “about-your”: both words strong, with a clear /j/ between them
“abou-yer”: the /t/ is dropped before the weak “your”
“abou-jyer”: the /t/ and the /j/ blend into /dʒ/
“abou-chyer”: the /t/ and a weak “your” blend into /tʃ/
quests.correctAnswer: “abou-chyer”: the /t/ and a weak “your” blend into /tʃ/
quests.hint: Look at how “about” ends and how weak “your” begins.
quests.explanation: “About” ends in /t/ and “your” begins with /j/, so the pair blends into /tʃ/: “abou-chyer”. “Me” is also weak here: /mi/. Interviewers say this opening line quickly and often, so the blend is very likely. Hearing it helps you start the answer without hesitation.
quests.phoneticRule: Interview prompts such as “tell me about your…” combine a weak “me” with a /t/ + /j/ blend at “about your”.
quests.spokenForm: So, tell mi abou-chyer last job

quests.instruction: An interviewer asks, “Right, why do you want to work here?” Which description of the quick form is most accurate?
quests.word: Right, why do you want to work here
quests.textToSpeak: Right, why do you want to work here
options: “why do you want to work here”, with every word equally strong and every sound separate
“why-chu wanna work here”: a /tʃ/ blend instead of /dʒ/
“why-dya wonta work here”: the /t/ of “want” is kept
“why-dja wanna work here”: a /dʒ/ blend plus “wanna”, with beats on why, work, here
quests.correctAnswer: “why-dja wanna work here”: a /dʒ/ blend plus “wanna”, with beats on why, work, here
quests.hint: Decide which words carry the beats, then look at the small words between them.
quests.explanation: “Do you” blends into /dʒə/ and “want to” reduces to “wanna”, so the question is built on three beats: “why”, “work” and “here”. A candidate who expects “do you want to” in full may miss the question. Recognising the shape lets you answer the real question.
quests.phoneticRule: A wh-question with “do you want to” is typically spoken with a /dʒə/ blend and the informal “wanna”, leaving only three stressed words.
quests.spokenForm: Right, why-dja wanna work here

quests.instruction: Which spoken form fits “Okay, could you describe a time you led a team?”
quests.word: Okay, could you describe a time you led a team
quests.textToSpeak: Okay, could you describe a time you led a team
options: “cou-ja” (a /dʒ/ blend), and “led a” linked as “le-da”
“could you” with a clear /j/, and “led a” with a pause between the words
“cou-cha” (a /tʃ/ blend), and “led a” linked
“cou-ja”, but “time you” also blends into /tʃ/
quests.correctAnswer: “cou-ja” (a /dʒ/ blend), and “led a” linked as “le-da”
quests.hint: Check which junctions have a /d/ or /t/ before /j/, and which have a consonant before a vowel.
quests.explanation: “Could you” has /d/ + /j/, so it blends into /dʒ/. “Led a” has a /d/ before a vowel, so it links. “Time you” ends in /m/, which does not blend with /j/. So the line has one blend and one link, and a possible blend that does not occur.
quests.phoneticRule: In a single interview question, only /t d s z/ junctions blend, and the other consonant-vowel junctions link.
quests.spokenForm: Okay, cou-ja describe a time you le-da team

quests.instruction: In a meeting someone says, “Right, I don’t think that’s going to work.” Which spoken form is typical?
quests.word: Right, I don’t think that’s going to work
quests.textToSpeak: Right, I don’t think that’s going to work
options: “do not think that is going to work”, with every word kept separate
“doan’ think that’s gonna work”: a weak /t/ and the informal “gonna”
“don-tuh think that’s gonna work”, with an extra vowel after the /t/ of “don’t”
“doan’ think that’s gonta work”, with the /t/ of “to” kept
quests.correctAnswer: “doan’ think that’s gonna work”: a weak /t/ and the informal “gonna”
quests.hint: Listen to how “don’t” ends before “think”, and how “going to” is said.
quests.explanation: “Don’t” keeps its /əʊ/ vowel and its final /t/ is weak before “think”. “Going to” is reduced to “gonna”. The disagreement is softened by the contractions, but the meaning is still clear. A listener expecting full words may think the speaker said something else.
quests.phoneticRule: Disagreement in meetings often uses contracted negatives and the informal “gonna”, with the key words stressed.
quests.spokenForm: Right, I doan’ think that’s gonna work

quests.instruction: Which spoken form fits “Absolutely, we’ve got to move quickly on this”?
quests.word: Absolutely, we’ve got to move quickly on this
quests.textToSpeak: Absolutely, we’ve got to move quickly on this
options: “we’ve gotta”: “we’ve” is one syllable and “got to” becomes “gotta”
“we have got to”: three full words with a clear /h/ and no contraction
“we’ve gonna”: “got to” becomes “gonna” in the same way as “going to”
“we’ve got-too”: a strong “to” after “got”
quests.correctAnswer: “we’ve gotta”: “we’ve” is one syllable and “got to” becomes “gotta”
quests.hint: Combine what you know about “’ve” and “got to”.
quests.explanation: “We’ve” is a standard contraction of “we have”: one syllable, /wiːv/. “Got to” is reduced to the informal “gotta”: /ˈɡɒtə/. Together they sound like “wee-v gotta”. The agreement is strong and quick, which suits the spoken form.
quests.phoneticRule: A contracted “’ve” and the informal “gotta” frequently occur together in agreeing or urging statements.
quests.spokenForm: Absolutely, we’ve gotta move quickly on this

quests.instruction: Which features are heard in “Well, they could’ve told us earlier”?
quests.word: Well, they could’ve told us earlier
quests.textToSpeak: Well, they could’ve told us earlier
options: “could have” with a strong “have”, and “told us” separated
“could of” with a full /ɒv/, and “told us” linked
“cou-dəv”, but “told us” with the /d/ dropped
“could’ve” as /ˈkʊdəv/ and “told us” linked as “tol-dus”
quests.correctAnswer: “could’ve” as /ˈkʊdəv/ and “told us” linked as “tol-dus”
quests.hint: Check how “could’ve” ends and what the /d/ of “told” does before “us”.
quests.explanation: “Could’ve” is two syllables with a weak /əv/: /ˈkʊdəv/. “Told us” has a /d/ before a vowel, so the /d/ links onto “us”: “tol-dus”. A polite complaint like this often combines a contraction with a link. It should be written “could have”, not “could of”.
quests.phoneticRule: A modal + ’ve contraction is followed by a normal consonant-to-vowel link at the next boundary.
quests.spokenForm: Well, they cou-dəv tol-dus earlier

quests.instruction: Which spoken form of “sent you” fits “Anyway, I’m calling about the email I sent you”?
quests.word: Anyway, I’m calling about the email I sent you
quests.textToSpeak: Anyway, I’m calling about the email I sent you
options: “sent-you”: both sounds are separate, with a clear /j/
“sen-jew”: they blend into /dʒ/ instead
“sen-chew”: the /t/ and /j/ blend into /tʃ/
“sen-shoo”: they blend into /ʃ/ instead
quests.correctAnswer: “sen-chew”: the /t/ and /j/ blend into /tʃ/
quests.hint: Name the final consonant of “sent”, then think about what it does before “you”.
quests.explanation: “Sent” ends in /t/ and “you” begins with /j/, so they blend into /tʃ/: “sen-chew”. The /n/ stays. Because “you” ends the clause, it is a bit more prominent than usual, but the blend still occurs. The phone version of an email follow-up often contains this blend.
quests.phoneticRule: Verbs ending in /t/ blend with a following “you” even in clause-final position.
quests.spokenForm: Anyway, I’m calling about the email I sen-chew

quests.instruction: Which features are heard in “Basically, did you get a chance to read it?”
quests.word: Basically, did you get a chance to read it
quests.textToSpeak: Basically, did you get a chance to read it
options: A /tʃ/ blend (“did you”), a dropped /t/, and a strong “to” in “chance to read”
A /dʒ/ blend (“did you”), a linked /t/ (“get a”), a weak “to”
A /dʒ/ blend, an intrusive /r/, and a strong “to”
No blend, because “did” ends in a vowel
quests.correctAnswer: A /dʒ/ blend (“did you”), a linked /t/ (“get a”), a weak “to”
quests.hint: Go through the first half of the question boundary by boundary.
quests.explanation: “Did you” has /d/ + /j/, so it blends into /dʒ/. “Get a” has a /t/ before a vowel, so it links. “To” is a weak function word: /tə/. The stressed words are “get”, “chance” and “read”. Together they make the question quick and polite.
quests.phoneticRule: A polite follow-up question combines a /dʒ/ blend, a link and a weak “to” in one chunk.
quests.spokenForm: Basically, di-ja ge-ta chance tuh read it

quests.instruction: Which spoken form of “perhaps your” fits “Perhaps your assistant could forward it to me”?
quests.word: Perhaps your assistant could forward it to me
quests.textToSpeak: Perhaps your assistant could forward it to me
options: “perhaps-your”: both words strong, with a clear /j/
“perha-zhyer”: they blend into /ʒ/
“perha-chyer”: they blend into /tʃ/
“perha-shyer”: the /s/ and a weak “your” blend into /ʃ/
quests.correctAnswer: “perha-shyer”: the /s/ and a weak “your” blend into /ʃ/
quests.hint: Find the final consonant of “perhaps” and predict its blend with a weak “your”.
quests.explanation: “Perhaps” ends in /s/, and “your” begins with /j/, so the pair blends into /ʃ/: “perha-shyer”. The /p/ before the /s/ stays. A polite suggestion made by phone often begins this way, so the blend is typical.
quests.phoneticRule: A voiceless /s/ before a weak “your” gives the voiceless blend /ʃ/, even when preceded by another consonant.
quests.spokenForm: Perha-shyer assistant could forward it to me

quests.instruction: Which sound is likely omitted in “Unfortunately, the next deadline is on Friday”?
quests.word: Unfortunately, the next deadline is on Friday
quests.textToSpeak: Unfortunately, the next deadline is on Friday
options: The /d/ of “deadline”, at the start of the word
The /t/ of “next”, before the consonant /d/
The /n/ of “deadline”, before “is”
The /z/ of “is”, before “on”
quests.correctAnswer: The /t/ of “next”, before the consonant /d/
quests.hint: Look for a /t/ that sits between other consonants before another word.
quests.explanation: “Next” ends in /kst/, and “deadline” begins with /d/, so the /t/ is wedged between /s/ and /d/ and is often omitted: “nex’ deadline”. The other candidates are either word-initial or followed by a vowel. Spotting the right /t/ is the key.
quests.phoneticRule: A /t/ between /s/ and a following consonant is the most likely elision site in deadline talk.
quests.spokenForm: Unfortunately, the nex’ deadline is on Friday

quests.instruction: Which /t/ sounds are likely omitted in “Clearly, we just missed the last milestone”?
quests.word: Clearly, we just missed the last milestone
quests.textToSpeak: Clearly, we just missed the last milestone
options: The /s/ of “just” and the /s/ of “last”, which sit before consonants
The /t/ of “last” only, because “just” links onto the next word
The /t/ of “just” and the /t/ of “last”, each before a consonant
None: elision is not possible in a formal meeting
quests.correctAnswer: The /t/ of “just” and the /t/ of “last”, each before a consonant
quests.hint: Find the two word-final /t/ sounds that sit after /s/ and before another consonant.
quests.explanation: “Just” ends in /st/ before /m/, and “last” ends in /st/ before /m/. Both /t/ sounds sit in crowded clusters and are often omitted: “jus’ missed the las’ milestone”. Formal meetings use connected speech as much as casual ones, so this elision is normal.
quests.phoneticRule: Elision applies in formal meetings as well as casual speech, wherever a /t/ is wedged between /s/ and a consonant.
quests.spokenForm: Clearly, we jus’ missed the las’ milestone

quests.instruction: Which process changes the /t/ in “tight budget” in “Okay, it’s a tight budget for the next quarter”?
quests.word: Okay, it’s a tight budget for the next quarter
quests.textToSpeak: Okay, it’s a tight budget for the next quarter
options: Elision: the /t/ is omitted before the /b/
Coalescence: the /t/ blends with the /b/ into /tʃ/
Linking: the /t/ moves onto “budget”
Assimilation: the /t/ shifts toward /p/ before the /b/
quests.correctAnswer: Assimilation: the /t/ shifts toward /p/ before the /b/
quests.hint: Ask whether the /t/ disappears, moves, blends or changes place.
quests.explanation: “Tight” ends in /t/ before the lip sound /b/, so the /t/ can shift toward the lips: “taip budget”. It is not omitted, because it is still heard in a changed form. It does not blend into /tʃ/, because there is no /j/. In the same sentence “next quarter” has a different process, an omitted /t/.
quests.phoneticRule: A /t/ before a bilabial consonant assimilates in place, whereas a /t/ in a cluster before a non-matching consonant may be omitted.
quests.spokenForm: Okay, it’s a taip budget for the nex’ quarter

quests.instruction: Which links are heard in “So, can anyone give an example of that?”
quests.word: So, can anyone give an example of that
quests.textToSpeak: So, can anyone give an example of that
options: Only “can anyone” links, while the other two boundaries keep a clear break between the words
A linking /r/ in “give an”, and a glide in “example of”
Each consonant links: /n/ in “can anyone”, /v/ in “give an”, /l/ in “example of”
Elision in “can anyone”, and gemination in “give an”
quests.correctAnswer: Each consonant links: /n/ in “can anyone”, /v/ in “give an”, /l/ in “example of”
quests.hint: Check each word that ends in a consonant before a vowel-initial word.
quests.explanation: “Can” ends in /n/ before “anyone”, “give” ends in /v/ before “an”, and “example” ends in /l/ before “of”. Each consonant is followed by a vowel, so each links: “ca-nanyone gi-van example-ləv”. A seminar question is a good place to practise hearing a long chain of links.
quests.phoneticRule: A chain of consonant + vowel boundaries produces a series of links, each independent of the others.
quests.spokenForm: So, ca-nanyone gi-van example-ləv that

quests.instruction: Which consonants link in “Actually, I’d like to add a point about it”?
quests.word: Actually, I’d like to add a point about it
quests.textToSpeak: Actually, I’d like to add a point about it
options: “add a” (/d/), “point about” (/t/) and “about it” (/t/)
Only the /d/ of “add”; the others are separated
The /k/ of “like” onto “to”, and the /t/ of “to” onto “add”
None: academic speech avoids linking
quests.correctAnswer: “add a” (/d/), “point about” (/t/) and “about it” (/t/)
quests.hint: Underline each word-final consonant that comes before a word beginning with a vowel.
quests.explanation: “Add a”, “point about” and “about it” each have a consonant before a vowel, so they link. “Like to” has /k/ before /t/, and “to add” has /t/ before a vowel, but “to” is a weak word, so the /t/ also links in most speech. The key idea is that seminar language is as connected as any other.
quests.phoneticRule: Academic speech uses linking as freely as informal speech, wherever a consonant precedes a vowel-initial word.
quests.spokenForm: Actually, I’d like tuh a-da poin-tabou-tit

quests.instruction: Which /r/ may appear in “Perhaps we could go back to the idea of equality?”
quests.word: Perhaps we could go back to the idea of equality
quests.textToSpeak: Perhaps we could go back to the idea of equality
options: An intrusive /r/ in “idea of”, in accents that use it
A linking /r/ in “idea of”, because of the spelling
An intrusive /r/ in “back to”
No /r/ is possible in any accent
quests.correctAnswer: An intrusive /r/ in “idea of”, in accents that use it
quests.hint: Check whether “idea” has an “r” in its spelling, and remember that this feature is accent-dependent.
quests.explanation: “Idea” ends in /ə/ with no “r” in the spelling, so an /r/ before “of” would be intrusive, not linking. Many non-rhotic speakers use it; rhotic speakers do not. “Back to” has a /k/ before a consonant and offers no site for /r/. Recognition matters more than production.
quests.phoneticRule: An /r/ before “of” after “idea” is intrusive (not linking) because there is no “r” in the spelling, and it is accent-dependent.
quests.spokenForm: Perhaps we could go back to the idea-rof equality

quests.instruction: Which spoken form fits “Alright, who’s going to do the slides?”
quests.word: Alright, who’s going to do the slides
quests.textToSpeak: Alright, who’s going to do the slides
options: “who is going to do the slides”, with all words strong and separate
“who’s gonna do the slides”: “gonna” for “going to”, and a weak “the”
“who’s gonna do-too the slides”, with a strong “to”
“whose gonna do the slides”: a different word, “whose”
quests.correctAnswer: “who’s gonna do the slides”: “gonna” for “going to”, and a weak “the”
quests.hint: Notice how “who’s” and “going to” are said, and how strong “the” is.
quests.explanation: “Who’s” is a contraction of “who is”, and it sounds the same as “whose”, so context decides. “Going to” is reduced to “gonna”, and “the” is weak: /ðə/. The key words are “who” and “slides”. A group chat often moves this fast.
quests.phoneticRule: A group question about tasks combines a homophonous contraction (“who’s”), the informal “gonna” and a weak “the”.
quests.spokenForm: Alright, who’s gonna do the slides

quests.instruction: Which words are weak in “Fine, I’ll write the intro and you can do the rest”?
quests.word: Fine, I’ll write the intro and you can do the rest
quests.textToSpeak: Fine, I’ll write the intro and you can do the rest
options: “write”, “intro” and “rest”: the meaning words
Only “and” and “can”, because they are short
“the”, “and”, “you”, “can” and “the”: the grammar words
All words are equally strong in a group chat
quests.correctAnswer: “the”, “and”, “you”, “can” and “the”: the grammar words
quests.hint: Find the words that carry the plan, and see which are only grammar.
quests.explanation: The stressed words are “write”, “intro” and “rest”, with a lighter beat on “do”. The small words “the”, “and”, “you”, “can” and “the” are reduced: /ði/, /n/, /jə/, /kən/ and /ðə/. Hearing them as quiet lets the plan stand out.
quests.phoneticRule: In a division of tasks, content words carry the beats, and the pronouns, articles and auxiliaries are weak.
quests.spokenForm: Fine, I’ll write thee intro n yuh kən do thuh rest

quests.instruction: Which words are weak in “Anyway, I’ll send it to the group by Friday”?
quests.word: Anyway, I’ll send it to the group by Friday
quests.textToSpeak: Anyway, I’ll send it to the group by Friday
options: “send”, “group” and “Friday”, while “it”, “to”, “the” and “by” carry the beats
Only “to” and “by”, because they are prepositions
None, because group chats avoid reductions
“it”, “to”, “the” and “by”, while “send”, “group” and “Friday” carry the beats
quests.correctAnswer: “it”, “to”, “the” and “by”, while “send”, “group” and “Friday” carry the beats
quests.hint: Pick out the verb, the group and the deadline, and treat everything else as quiet.
quests.explanation: The message is “send… group… Friday”. The small words “it”, “to”, “the” and “by” are weak, and “it” links to the /d/ of “send”: “sen-dit tuh thuh group buh Friday”. Group chats are casual, so reduced forms are the norm.
quests.phoneticRule: A plan statement keeps the same weak forms as other speech, with stress on the verb, the noun and the deadline.
quests.spokenForm: Anyway, I’ll sen-dit tuh thuh group buh Friday

quests.instruction: Which sounds are likely omitted in “West coast trains are delayed this morning”?
quests.word: West coast trains are delayed this morning
quests.textToSpeak: West coast trains are delayed this morning
options: The /s/ of “west” and the /s/ of “coast”, which sit before consonants
The /t/ of “west” before /k/, and the /t/ of “coast” before /t/
The /k/ of “coast” and the /t/ of “trains”
None: announcements are fully articulated in every case
quests.correctAnswer: The /t/ of “west” before /k/, and the /t/ of “coast” before /t/
quests.hint: Look for word-final /st/ clusters followed by a consonant.
quests.explanation: “West” ends in /st/ before /k/, and “coast” ends in /st/ before /t/. Both /t/ sounds are in crowded clusters and are often omitted: “wes’ coas’ trains”. Even careful announcements show this, though slow ones may keep the /t/. The pattern is useful to know when you hear delays.
quests.phoneticRule: Word-final /st/ clusters lose the /t/ before a consonant even in public announcements, though careful speech may retain it.
quests.spokenForm: Wes’ coas’ trains are delayed this morning

quests.instruction: Which sound is often omitted in “Pardon me, is the next stop Victoria?”
quests.word: Pardon me, is the next stop Victoria
quests.textToSpeak: Pardon me, is the next stop Victoria
options: The /t/ of “next”, before the /s/ of “stop”
The /s/ of “next”, before the /s/ of “stop”
The /k/ of “next”, before the /s/
The /t/ of “stop”, at the end of the word
quests.correctAnswer: The /t/ of “next”, before the /s/ of “stop”
quests.hint: Compare the sounds on either side of the /t/ in “next”.
quests.explanation: “Next” ends in /kst/ before “stop”, which begins with /s/. The /t/ sits between /s/ and /s/ and is often omitted: “nex’ stop”. The two /s/ sounds then merge. A passenger who listens for “next stop” may hear only “nex’ stop”.
quests.phoneticRule: A /t/ between /s/ and a following /s/ is omitted frequently, leaving a lengthened /s/.
quests.spokenForm: Pardon me, is the nex’ stop Victoria

quests.instruction: Which sound is often missing in a fast “Mind the gap between the train and the platform”?
quests.word: Mind the gap between the train and the platform
quests.textToSpeak: Mind the gap between the train and the platform
options: The /d/ of “mind”, before the weak “the”
The /g/ of “gap”, at the start of the word
The /t/ of “between”, in the middle of the word
The /n/ of “and”, before “the”
quests.correctAnswer: The /d/ of “mind”, before the weak “the”
quests.hint: Look for a word-final stop in a cluster before a weak word.
quests.explanation: “Mind” ends in /nd/ before the weak “the”, so the /d/ is often left out: “min’ the gap”. The other options are word-initial, word-medial or already part of a reduced “and”. The announcement is so frequent that you may hear only the /n/ and the vowel.
quests.phoneticRule: A word-final /d/ in an /nd/ cluster is a likely elision site before a following weak word.
quests.spokenForm: Min’ the gap between the train n the platform

quests.instruction: Which sound shifts in “Pardon me, how do I get to the main gate?”
quests.word: Pardon me, how do I get to the main gate
quests.textToSpeak: Pardon me, how do I get to the main gate
options: The /t/ of “get”, which shifts toward /g/
The /n/ of “main”, which shifts toward /ŋ/ before /g/
The /t/ of “to”, which shifts to /d/
The /m/ of “me”, which shifts to /n/
quests.correctAnswer: The /n/ of “main”, which shifts toward /ŋ/ before /g/
quests.hint: Look for a tongue-tip nasal before a back-of-the-mouth sound.
quests.explanation: “Main” ends in /n/ before “gate”, which begins with /g/, a back-of-the-mouth sound, so the /n/ can shift toward [ŋ]: “maing gate”. The /t/ of “get” links onto “to” and does not assimilate. Asking directions is full of place names that trigger this change.
quests.phoneticRule: A word-final /n/ before /g/ often assimilates to velar [ŋ], as in place names such as “main gate”.
quests.spokenForm: Pardon me, how do I get to the maing gate

quests.instruction: Which change is heard in “Hello, is it a ten minute walk from here?”
quests.word: Hello, is it a ten minute walk from here
quests.textToSpeak: Hello, is it a ten minute walk from here
options: The /t/ of “ten” shifts to /p/ before the /m/ of “minute”
The /n/ of “ten” shifts to /m/ before “minute”
The /m/ of “minute” shifts to /n/ to match “ten”
The /n/ of “ten” is omitted
quests.correctAnswer: The /n/ of “ten” shifts to /m/ before “minute”
quests.hint: Check what follows the /n/ and where in the mouth that sound is made.
quests.explanation: “Ten” ends in /n/ before “minute”, which begins with /m/, a lip sound, so the /n/ can shift to [m]: “tem minute”. The two /m/ sounds then run together. Distances are often given in tens of minutes, so this change is common in directions.
quests.phoneticRule: A word-final /n/ assimilates to [m] before a bilabial, as in “ten minutes” and similar distance expressions.
quests.spokenForm: Hello, is it a tem minute walk from here

quests.instruction: Which spoken form fits “Thanks, which road leads to the Queen Mary bridge?”
quests.word: Thanks, which road leads to the Queen Mary bridge
quests.textToSpeak: Thanks, which road leads to the Queen Mary bridge
options: “Queeng Mary”: the /n/ shifts to /ŋ/ before “Mary”
“Queen Mary”: the /n/ must stay a tongue-tip sound in every careful accent
“Queem Mary”: the /n/ of “Queen” shifts to /m/ before “Mary”
“Quee Mary”: the /n/ is omitted before “Mary”
quests.correctAnswer: “Queem Mary”: the /n/ of “Queen” shifts to /m/ before “Mary”
quests.hint: Match the nasal before “Mary” to the place of the next sound.
quests.explanation: “Queen” ends in /n/ before “Mary”, which begins with /m/, so the /n/ can shift to [m]: “Queem Mary”. A clear /n/ is also acceptable in careful speech. Place names are good examples because they are heard often in directions.
quests.phoneticRule: Place assimilation is common in proper names, where the final /n/ of the first word adapts to the next initial consonant.
quests.spokenForm: Thanks, which road leads to the Queem Mary bridge

quests.instruction: Which words are weak in “May I see your passport and boarding pass?”
quests.word: May I see your passport and boarding pass
quests.textToSpeak: May I see your passport and boarding pass
options: “I”, “your” and “and”: the function words
“passport” and “boarding”: the nouns
“see” and “pass”: the short words
All equally strong at a check-in desk
quests.correctAnswer: “I”, “your” and “and”: the function words
quests.hint: Find the nouns and the verb, then decide which small words are left.
quests.explanation: The key words are “see”, “passport” and “boarding pass”. The small words “I”, “your” and “and” are reduced: /aɪ/ or /ə/, /jə/ and /n/. A check-in agent says this many times a day, so the weak forms are very fast. Listening for the stressed words tells you what to hand over.
quests.phoneticRule: A check-in request keeps stress on the verb and the documents, and weakens the pronouns and conjunction.
quests.spokenForm: May I see yer passport n boarding pass

quests.instruction: How are “has been” and “by” pronounced in “Your flight has been delayed by about forty minutes”?
quests.word: Your flight has been delayed by about forty minutes
quests.textToSpeak: Your flight has been delayed by about forty minutes
options: “has” /hæz/, “been” /biːn/ and “by” /baɪ/, all strong
“has” weak, but “been” and “by” strong
“has” /əz/, “been” /bɪn/ and “by” /bə/, all weak
“has been” fused into one word, “hasben”
quests.correctAnswer: “has” /əz/, “been” /bɪn/ and “by” /bə/, all weak
quests.hint: Find the stressed words and ask what happens to the auxiliary stretch before “delayed”.
quests.explanation: The stressed words are “flight”, “delayed”, “forty” and “minutes”. “Has been” is a run of auxiliaries and is weak: /əz bɪn/, and “by” is reduced to /bə/. So the delay announcement is mostly weak words wrapped around four beats. Listening for the beats gives you the news.
quests.phoneticRule: In service announcements, a string of auxiliaries and a preposition is weak, leaving the content words prominent.
quests.spokenForm: Your flight həz bɪn delayed bə about forty minutes

quests.instruction: Which spoken form fits “Anything to declare at customs?”
quests.word: Anything to declare at customs
quests.textToSpeak: Anything to declare at customs
options: “Anything too declare at customs?”: both words strong
“Anythin’ declare customs?”: both words dropped
“Anything tuh declare at customs?”: “to” and “at” are weak
“Anythin-chu declare at customs?”: a blend of “anything” and “to”
quests.correctAnswer: “Anything tuh declare at customs?”: “to” and “at” are weak
quests.hint: Check how “to” and “at” are said between the content words.
quests.explanation: “Anything”, “declare” and “customs” carry the beats. “To” is weak, /tə/, and “at” is weak, /ət/. Dropping them would change the grammar, and stressing them would slow the question. A customs officer says this quickly, so the weak forms are the norm.
quests.phoneticRule: A customs question keeps its function words in weak form between the stressed words.
quests.spokenForm: Anything tuh declare at customs

quests.instruction: Which features are heard in “Apologies, could I get a return ticket to Leeds?”
quests.word: Apologies, could I get a return ticket to Leeds
quests.textToSpeak: Apologies, could I get a return ticket to Leeds
options: “could I” (/d/ links onto “I”), “get a” (/t/ links onto “a”), and a weak “to”
A /dʒ/ blend in “could I”, a dropped /t/ in “get a”, and a strong “to” before the place name
A linking /r/ in “could I”, a glide in “get a”, and a weak “to”
Gemination in “could I”, assimilation in “get a”, and a strong “to”
quests.correctAnswer: “could I” (/d/ links onto “I”), “get a” (/t/ links onto “a”), and a weak “to”
quests.hint: Go through the request boundary by boundary, and say which processes apply.
quests.explanation: “Could” ends in /d/ before the vowel of “I”, so the /d/ links. “Get” ends in /t/ before the weak “a”, so the /t/ links. “To” is weak: /tə/. The stressed words are “get”, “return”, “ticket” and “Leeds”. A ticket request is a good stage check because it needs all three ideas.
quests.phoneticRule: A realistic request combines consonant-to-vowel linking at two boundaries with a weak “to” before the destination.
quests.spokenForm: Apologies, cou-dai ge-ta return ticket tuh Leeds

quests.instruction: Which features are heard in “Basically, we’re running out of time and need to decide”?
quests.word: Basically, we’re running out of time and need to decide
quests.textToSpeak: Basically, we’re running out of time and need to decide
options: Only a contraction; the rest is fully separated
Coalescence in “out of” and elision in “time”
A linking /r/ in “we’re”, and assimilation in “running out” before the vowel
A contraction (“we’re”), linking, the informal “outta”, and a weak “to”
quests.correctAnswer: A contraction (“we’re”), linking, the informal “outta”, and a weak “to”
quests.hint: List the reductions you know and check which appear in each stretch.
quests.explanation: “We’re” is a standard contraction. “Running out” links the /ŋ/ or /n/ onto “out”, and “out of” becomes “outta”. “And” is /n/ and “to” is /tə/. The stressed words are “running”, “time”, “need” and “decide”. A busy meeting often sounds like this.
quests.phoneticRule: A realistic meeting line combines standard contractions, informal reductions and weak forms in one clause.
quests.spokenForm: Basically, we’re runnin’ outta time n need tuh decide

quests.instruction: Which analysis fits “Apparently, the last bus left ten minutes ago”?
quests.word: Apparently, the last bus left ten minutes ago
quests.textToSpeak: Apparently, the last bus left ten minutes ago
options: Assimilation (“last bus”), elision (“ten minutes”) and coalescence (“minutes ago”)
Linking (“last bus”), gemination (“ten minutes”) and elision (“minutes ago”)
Elision (“last bus”), assimilation (“ten minutes”) and linking (“minutes ago”)
Elision (“last bus”), coalescence (“ten minutes”) and an intrusive /r/ (“minutes ago”)
quests.correctAnswer: Elision (“last bus”), assimilation (“ten minutes”) and linking (“minutes ago”)
quests.hint: Take the three boundaries one by one and ask what follows each word-final consonant.
quests.explanation: “Last bus” has a /t/ between /s/ and /b/, so it is often omitted. “Ten minutes” has /n/ before /m/, so it can assimilate to [m]. “Minutes ago” has /s/ before a vowel, so it links. The three boundaries show three different processes, and recognising each is the aim of the stage.
quests.phoneticRule: A single travel complaint can show elision, assimilation and linking at three successive boundaries.
quests.spokenForm: Apparently, the las’ bus left tem minutes ago
